title: Why Do Onions Make You Cry After 30 Seconds? 🧅
description:
Why do onions make you cry? Cutting an onion mixes a sulfur compound with an enzyme, and a second enzyme (found in 2002) turns the result into syn-propanethial-S-oxide, an irritating gas that peaks about 30 seconds after the cut and makes your tear glands wash it away.

topic: Why do onions make you cry?
script: Onions fire tear gas at your eyes, 30 seconds after you cut them. How? Inside every onion cell, two chemicals are kept apart, in separate little rooms. One is a sulfur molecule. The other is an enzyme. Your knife smashes the walls, and they finally mix. The enzyme turns the sulfur into an acid, then a second enzyme, only discovered in 2002, flips that acid into a gas. It drifts up, and peaks about 30 seconds after the cut. When it hits your eyes, tiny nerves shout "burning!" So your tear glands flood your eyes, to wash it away. Why bother? It's armor. Any animal that bites an onion, gets a face full of sting. Want fewer tears? Cut it under running water. So, would you still eat a plant that fights back with tear gas?
key_facts: Onion cells keep sulfur-containing amino acid sulfoxides and the enzyme alliinase apart until the cell is damaged
Alliinase turns the sulfoxides into sulfenic acids
Lachrymatory factor synthase, reported in Nature in 2002 (Imai et al.), converts the sulfenic acid into syn-propanethial-S-oxide
The tear-causing compound peaks about 30 seconds after the onion is cut
Corneal nerve endings sense it as burning and tear glands wash it away
Cutting under running water reduces exposure
